# Core Inferential Methods {.unnumbered}

Inference uses observed data to learn about a quantity beyond the sample. Its validity depends on the study design and analysis assumptions. Increasing sample size can reduce sampling uncertainty, but it does not by itself remove a systematic error in how participants were selected or measurements were obtained.

This part begins with estimates, confidence intervals, p-values, errors, and power. It then considers continuous outcomes in two or more groups and associations between categorical variables. Throughout, define the target quantity before selecting the test: a mean difference, a distributional comparison, a proportion, or a ratio.

The p-value and confidence interval provide different information. The p-value refers to the incompatibility of the observed data with a specified null model. The interval communicates estimation uncertainty under its assumptions. Neither replaces the magnitude of the estimate or the clinical question. [@ASAp; @NISTCI]

By the end of this part, the reader should be able to choose a basic independent or paired comparison, check the relevant assumptions, interpret uncertainty, and avoid treating a non-significant result as proof that two groups are equivalent.
